'''''Eucalyptus polyanthemos''''', commonly known as '''red box''',<ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20polyanthemos |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=4 December 2019}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree, that is 
native to eastern Australia but has been introduced into other countries. It has fibrous bark on the trunk and larger branches, smooth greyish to cream-coloured bark above, or smooth bark throughout. It has broadly egg-shaped to round juvenile leaves, lance-shaped, egg-shaped or almost round adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven, white flowers and barrel-shaped to conical fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|20|m}} but does not form a [[lignotuber]]. It has fibrous or flaky bark on the trunk and larger branches, smooth mottled greyish, cream-coloured and yellow bark above, or sometimes smooth bark throughout. It often has a crooked trunk and is noted for its domed canopy of greyish foliage. Leaves on young plants are green to bluish grey, broadly egg-shaped to more or less round, {{cvt|25-80|mm}} long and {{cvt|25-65|mm}} wide and [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]]. [[Crown (botany)|Crown]] leaves are the same shade of dull green to bluish or greyish on both sides, lance-shaped to egg-shaped or round, {{cvt|50-110|mm}} long and {{cvt|18-50|mm}} wide tapering to a petiole {{cvt|10-27|mm}} long. Veins on the leaves are distinct and the marginal vein is notably distant from the leaf edge.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name=Costermans>{{cite book|author=Costermans, L.| title=Native Trees and Shrubs of South-eastern Australia |publisher=Rigby|location=Australia | year=1981 | isbn=0-7270-1403-X}}</ref><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' subsp. ''polyanthemos'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_polyanthemos_subsp._polyanthemos.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=30 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~polyanthemos |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=4 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/b5562066-fc53-4d62-8927-03ecfd50e1fe |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Victoria |access-date=4 December 2019}}</ref>

The flower buds are arranged on the ends of branchlets in groups of seven on a branching [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2-10|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|1-5|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to diamond-shaped, {{cvt|3-5|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-3|mm}} wide with a conical to slightly beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs in October and November (spring in Australia) and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, barrel-shaped to conical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-6|mm}} long and wide with the valves below the level of the rim.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="Costermans" /><ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' was first formally described in 1843 by [[Johannes Conrad Schauer|Johannes Schauer]] in [[Wilhelm Gerhard Walpers|Walpers']] book ''Repertorium Botanices Systematicae''. This description was based on  the [[type specimen]] which was collected in 1822 near [[Bathurst, New South Wales|Bathurst]] by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos''|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455850|publisher=APNI|access-date=4 December 2019}}{{Dead link|date=March 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="Walpers">{{cite book |editor=Wilhelm Gerhard Walpers |author=Johannes Conrad Schauer |title=Repertorium Botanices Systematicae (Volume 2) |date=1843 |publisher=Sumtibus Frederici Hofmeister |location=New York |page=924 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/32093#page/940/mode/1up |access-date=4 December 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''polyanthemos'') is from the [[ancient Greek]] ''poly-'' meaning "many" and ''anthemon'' meaning "flower'.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Subspecies ''longior'' is found in taller forest in the foothills of far eastern Victoria.<ref name="RBGV1" />  Subspecies ''marginalis'' is also found in Victoria, between the [[Greater Bendigo National Park]] and [[Stawell, Victoria|Stawell]] with outliers near [[Bacchus Marsh]]. It grows in forest or woodland in dry, gravelly soils.<ref name="RBGV2" />

Subspecies ''polyanthemos'' grows on the slopes and tablelands of central and southern New South Wales  where it is widespread on the central and southern slopes and tablelands.<ref name="RBGS1" /> Subspecies ''vestita'' is found in Victoria and New South Wales. It grows in woodland south from [[Gulgong, New South Wales|Gulgong]] but with a small outlier population in the upper [[Hunter Valley]]. It is widespread in Victoria east of [[Ararat, Victoria|Ararat]], growing on poor stony soils, usually on ridges and slopes.<ref name="RBGV4" />

==Ecology==
The larvae of the moth species ''[[Trichiocercus sparshalli]]'' and the eucalyptus leaf mining sawfly ''[[Phylacteophaga froggatti]]'' feed on the leaves.<ref>{{cite web|author=Herbison-Evans, Don and Stella Crossley|title=''Trichiocercus sparshalli'' (Curtis, 1830) |work=Caterpillars: especially Australian ones |url=http://linus.socs.uts.edu.au/~don/larvae/noto/sparsh.html |access-date=2008-03-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080726194832/http://linus.socs.uts.edu.au/~don/larvae/noto/sparsh.html |archive-date=2008-07-26 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Eucalyptus leaf mining sawfly|url=http://www.ensisjv.com/ResearchCapabilitiesAchievements/ForestHealthBiosecurityandFire/ForestPestFactSheet/Eucalyptusleafminingsawfly/tabid/346/Default.aspx|publisher=ensis|access-date=2008-03-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071220183422/http://www.ensisjv.com/ResearchCapabilitiesAchievements/ForestHealthBiosecurityandFire/ForestPestFactSheet/Eucalyptusleafminingsawfly/tabid/346/Default.aspx|archive-date=2007-12-20}}</ref> Large, old trees may form hollows that are used as nests for owls including the barking owl (''[[Ninox connivens]]'').<ref>{{cite web|title=Barking Owl-profile|url=http://threatenedspecies.environment.nsw.gov.au/tsprofile/profile.aspx?id=10561|publisher=Department of Environment and Climate Change NSW|access-date=2008-03-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080805121103/http://www.threatenedspecies.environment.nsw.gov.au/tsprofile/profile.aspx?id=10561|archive-date=2008-08-05}}</ref>

It has been recorded as an invasive species in [[California]].<ref name =nps>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos'' |url=http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/map/eupo1.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20061011235141/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/map/eupo1.htm|archive-date=October 11, 2006|work=Weeds Gone Wild|publisher=Plant Conservation Alliance|access-date=2008-03-20}}</ref> It is an [[introduced species]] in [[California]] where it is known as silver dollar gum, redbox or redbox gum.

==Significant trees==
A red box in [[Fraser National Park]] is recorded on the Significant Tree Register of the [[National Trust of Australia]] in Victoria. It is an unusual form with contorted limbs which is estimated to be around 80 years old and is 26.7 metres high.<ref>{{cite web |title=Register|url=http://vhd.heritage.vic.gov.au/search/nt_search?nspn=Eucalyptus+polyanthemos|publisher=National Trust of Australia - Victoria|access-date=2025-02-15}}</ref>

In [[Gilmore, Australian Capital Territory|Gilmore]] in the Australian Capital Territory, a tree known as Murumbeeja Scarred Red Box No 1 is listed on the [[Register of the National Estate]]. It is a [[scarred trees|scarred tree]], marking the removal by [[Indigenous Australians]] of bark, probably for [[canoe]] construction.<ref>
{{Cite AHPI|RNE18767|Murumbeeja Scarred Red Box No 1|accessdate=2008-03-21}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Use in horticulture===
The species is noted for its drought tolerance.<ref name=Metro/> Although usually considered to be slow growing, newly planted trees may have their growth rate enhanced with improved soil, good drainage and irrigation in the first two years.<ref name=Metro>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus polyanthemos''|url=http://www.metrotrees.com.au/treehandbook/page-listings/eucalyptus-polyanthemos.html|publisher=Metro Trees|access-date=2008-03-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080316191320/http://www.metrotrees.com.au/treehandbook/page-listings/eucalyptus-polyanthemos.html|archive-date=2008-03-16}}</ref> The species is moderately resistant to ''[[Armillaria]]'' root rot.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plants Resistant or Susceptible to ''Armillaria mellea'', The Oak Root Fungus |url=https://mgsantaclara.ucanr.edu/files/244383.pdf |author=Robert D. Raabe |publisher=Department of Environmental Science and Management, University of California, Berkeley }}</ref> A minimum temperature of −10 °C (15 °F) is required for cultivation.<ref>{{cite book|author=Smith, Ken|title=Western Home Landscaping|url=https://archive.org/details/westernhomelands00smit|url-access=registration|publisher=HP Books|year=1978|isbn=0-89586-012-0}}</ref>

===Use in floristry===
The juvenile foliage is used in [[floral arrangement]]s.<ref name=Jepson>{{cite web|title=''E. polyanthemos'' Schauer|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5179,5180,5185|work=The Jepson Manual Online|publisher=The Jepson Herbarium, University of California, Berkeley|access-date=2008-03-20}}</ref>

===Timber===
The timber is red in colour and is strong, hard and durable. It has been used for fence posts, railway sleepers and firewood.<ref name="ABRS" />
